date: text composed about 1330-1370 (the compiler dates an anecdote on f. 86r to 'seven hundred and thirty-odd' AH and writes to the Ibn Fadl Allah chancery circle); this copy is dated by Penn to the 15th century ('14--')
title: Ibn al-Qaysarani to the compiler of a Mamluk book of cipher correspondence: seven-line cipher note whose solution is lost with the end of the manuscript
place: Syria or Egypt (Mamluk chancery circle); Penn: Syria?
shelfmark: University of Pennsylvania, Kislak Center, LJS 51, f. 106v (OPenn image 0084_0217)
folio_note: f. 106v, lines 6-12: seven lines of invented signs, about 20 signs a line (roughly 120-130 signs), words divided by a dotted vertical stroke; three or four small red letters stand over the first signs of line 1; line 13 begins the compiler's 'I solved it at once and found he had made lam-alif ...' and the manuscript breaks off
status: Penn: 'encrypted correspondence between the compiler and various correspondents, in approximately 150 alphabets, accompanied by transcriptions of the letters in Arabic ... incomplete, lacking its beginning and end'. Page-by-page check of all 212 pages (15 Nov 2026): every other cipher passage is followed by its plaintext ('fa-halaltuhu ... wa-huwa' + the verses) or carries a red interlinear gloss; this last one lost its plaintext with the missing leaf. No study of the manuscript found. Not on DECODE.
why: The one cipher in the oldest surviving book of real Arabic cipher correspondence (14th-century Mamluk secretaries) that has no reading; about 200 solved siblings in the same volume show the conventions.
verify: Transcribe the seven lines from the OPenn master TIFF (2339 x 2959 px); use the red letters over line 1, the lam-alif hint, the word dividers and Arabic verse metre; compare the signs with the solved alphabets in ff. 1r-106r.

seen.cipher: Monoalphabetic-looking invented signs (loops, crossed strokes, figure-like shapes) with a dotted vertical word divider, introduced by the Arabic words 'wa-kataba li Ibn al-Qaysarani'. The line under the cipher starts the compiler's remark that he solved it at once and breaks off; the following leaf, which held the plaintext, is lost, so no decipherment is written on or with it.
